abstract.p: Multimodal freight operators allocate shipments across services with different capacities, fixed charges and delivery times. The economic value of additional capacity depends on which shipments can meet their deadlines on each service. This study investigates how capacity, service activation and delivery commitments jointly determine freight allocation and its sensitivity to cost errors. A path-based mixed-integer model was formulated for independently delivered shipment fractions. Evaluation covered a reference corridor, 2,997 capacity–deadline settings, 60 generated service catalogues, 50 paired capacity and fixed-charge settings, and 540 cost-error tests. Exact solutions were compared with sequential greedy allocation, multiple-order greedy allocation and activation search with linear-programming reallocation. Increasing reference rail capacity from 100 to 110 tonnes reduced cost from 4,380 to 4,140 currency units, whereas tightening one delivery deadline from 40 to 20 hours raised cost to 5,820. A maritime allocation cost 3,490 under 50-hour deadlines but became infeasible when uniform transit-time inflation exceeded 8.70%. Activation search matched 49 of the 60 exact objectives, with mean cost premiums of 0.00%–0.22% across catalogue sizes. With unit-cost errors bounded by 20%, mean realized regret was 2.89%, while 54.34% of tonnage was reassigned on average. The results show that capacity value depends on service eligibility and activation commitments, and that allocation changes need not produce comparable cost losses. The analysis provides a reproducible basis for evaluating capacity expansion, negotiating delivery commitments and prioritizing input verification in multimodal freight planning.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: A multimodal freight plan connects shipment requests with the transport and transfer services required for delivery. Road, rail and maritime alternatives differ in unit cost, transit time and available capacity. Selecting the lowest modal tariff is therefore insufficient to identify the least expensive feasible plan. Shared capacity can force part of a shipment onto a more expensive route, a delivery commitment can exclude a slower service, and a fixed transfer charge can make a low-volume movement uneconomic. These effects must be considered jointly because changing one restriction can alter the allocation of several shipments. This places the problem within operational analytics: the operator needs a defensible allocation of shipment quantities and service commitments, together with an explanation of the constraints driving cost [1], [2], [3], [4].

The decision context considered here is a freight forwarder or logistics platform allocating accepted shipments before dispatch. Quantities, origins, destinations and delivery windows are available at the planning epoch. The operator determines how much freight to assign to each eligible route and which transport or transfer operations to activate. Shipment fractions can travel independently, while the services they use draw on capacities shared with other commodities. The resulting plan must account for both quantity-dependent charges and the costs of opening additional services. Prices charged to customers, fleet acquisition and shipment acceptance remain outside this decision. This scope distinguishes operational allocation from simultaneous service-network design and pricing, where shipper choice and competitive responses also enter the model [5]. Recent operational synchromodal planning research likewise treats requests and available services as the starting point, but often adds real-time reassignment and coordination that are not assumed here [6].

Capacity restrictions and delivery commitments also determine how parameter errors affect a plan. A tariff error can reverse the ranking of feasible allocations, whereas a transit-time error can make a previously eligible service miss a shipment's deadline. These consequences require different assessments: realized cost can be evaluated on an unchanged feasible catalogue, but a delivery violation changes which allocations can be executed. Prediction-and-optimization research distinguishes downstream decision quality from prediction accuracy [7], [8], [9]. For freight planning, this distinction calls for evaluating the selected allocation together with the capacity and time restrictions supporting it.

Predictive models can update freight cost and time inputs [10], [11], while learned policies can assist mathematical-programming search [12], [13]. Both depend on an allocation model that connects the available information to operational constraints. A useful baseline must therefore establish which services are selected, how shared capacity is distributed and how the plan responds to input errors. These responses also identify where improved forecasts could affect decisions and where a conventional exact solver already provides an adequate computational solution.

The study addresses three connected research questions. How does shipment eligibility affect the marginal value of additional service capacity? Under what conditions do fixed activation charges reverse a choice suggested by modal unit rates? How do bounded unit-cost errors change the selected allocation and its realized cost? A single-epoch planning model provides a controlled setting for answering these questions. Holding the candidate catalogue fixed allows capacity, fixed charges and cost errors to be varied separately while retaining explicit delivery requirements.

The analysis combines a path-based fixed-charge formulation with analytical thresholds and computational experiments. A two-commodity corridor identifies capacity values and service-switching points, which are checked over a systematic capacity–deadline sweep. Generated service catalogues are then used to compare exact allocation with sequential greedy allocation, multiple-order greedy allocation and activation search with linear-programming reallocation. Paired experiments isolate capacity and fixed-charge effects without changing the other inputs. Finally, bounded-cost perturbations connect allocation changes and realized regret to a conservative error bound. The contribution is a reproducible account of when capacity expansion, deadline negotiation and parameter verification change an operational recommendation, using established optimization methods with explicit assumptions and decision measures.

The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews multimodal freight planning and the relationship between prediction, uncertainty and optimization. Section 3 defines the decision problem and mathematical formulation. Section 4 presents the analytical results and evaluation measures. Section 5 reports the experiments and results. Section 6 discusses operational implications and limitations, and Section 7 concludes.

sec.title: 2.1. Multimodal network planning and service decisions
sec.p: Multimodal freight planning draws on multicommodity flow and fixed-charge network-design models [1], [3], [4]. Their value is the explicit connection between shipment conservation, capacity use and service activation. Cost structures require particular care: quantity-dependent charges, fixed transfers and volume discounts represent different economic mechanisms. Established mixed-integer formulations for piecewise-linear and nonconvex costs show why these mechanisms should be modeled explicitly rather than absorbed into an ambiguous average tariff [14], [15]. The present study uses linear unit costs plus fixed activation charges; it does not assume quantity discounts.

Research has extended this core in several directions. Environmental service-network models jointly examine cost and modal shift [2], while travel-time uncertainty has been incorporated directly into intermodal network design [16]. Recent contributions address mixed-objective fleet planning [17], passenger access chains [18], emergency road–rail scheduling with transfer sequencing [19] and dynamic multimodal emergency operations involving drones [20]. These studies illustrate that the correct formulation depends on the actual decision boundary. Passenger connections, emergency sequencing and drone dispatch cannot be represented simply by relabeling a static freight allocation model.

More closely related studies address integrated corridor design and pricing [5], coordinated routing and storage over multiple periods [21] and robust multimodal hub design under budgeted demand uncertainty [22]. These strategic and temporal structures broaden the decision context. The single-epoch allocation studied here instead isolates capacity values and service-eligibility transitions while holding the candidate catalogue fixed.

sec.title: 2.2. Prediction and uncertainty in operational optimization
sec.p: Reviews of freight and logistics applications document the use of machine learning for forecasting and operational estimation [10], [11]. In a predict-then-optimize system, such estimates become inputs to a constrained decision model. The resulting decisions depend on where errors occur, not only on their average magnitude. An error on a rarely selected service may have little effect, whereas a small error near a route-ranking or deadline threshold can change the allocation.

Smart predict-then-optimize and decision-focused learning formalize this distinction between predictive loss and decision loss [7], [8]. Contextual optimization surveys organize methods for combining side information, uncertainty and optimization [9], while constraint-learning research emphasizes validation of the complete decision model after learned components have been embedded [23]. These contributions support evaluating the downstream allocation, rather than inferring operational value from prediction accuracy alone.

Recent transport studies provide application-specific combinations of these ideas. Filom and Razavi [24] combine prediction, uncertainty quantification and robust optimization for synchromodal freight. Tang et al. [25] use calibrated uncertainty sets for route planning, and Jia et al. [26] connect scenario prediction with online inventory routing. Building on this decision-oriented perspective, the present study tests the interaction of shared capacity, fixed activation charges and delivery eligibility, and examines how bounded input errors affect the resulting allocation.

sec.title: 2.3. Exact optimization and computational comparisons
sec.p: Machine learning has been used to assist branching, primal heuristics and other solver tasks [12], [13], [27]. Reinforcement-learning research also covers end-to-end combinatorial decisions [28]; DeepFreight combines learned dispatch with subsequent optimization [29], while forecast-assisted branch-and-price uses predictions within liner-shipping planning [30]. These approaches address different stages of the decision process. Their relevance here is the need for an explicit exact-solver baseline and a separation between parameter estimation and computational search.

Commodity order affects which shipments obtain scarce inexpensive capacity, and a feasible greedy assignment can be improved by reallocating flows after the services have been selected. Recent logistics studies also rely on metaheuristic search, including a clustering-based genetic algorithm for vehicle routing with time windows [31] and an interval-programming supply-chain model with capacitated facility selection solved by particle swarm, genetic and simulated-annealing algorithms [32]. Such methods are useful for larger instances, but their solution quality is easier to interpret when an exact reference is available on comparable instances. The computational design therefore compares exact allocation with sequential greedy allocation, multiple-order greedy allocation and activation search with linear-programming reallocation. All methods use the same costs, quantities, eligible services and capacity limits.

sec.title: 2.4. Decision interactions examined in this study
sec.p: The study focuses on three interactions that a modal-rate comparison cannot resolve. Capacity value depends on shipment eligibility; activating an additional inexpensive service can cost more than a small residual road allocation; and cost errors can change tonnage assignments without producing equally large objective losses. Table 1 identifies the decision boundary relative to related work. Sections 4–5 translate these interactions into thresholds, paired experiments and reproducible comparisons.

sec.title: 4.3. Planning and managerial acceptance
sec.p: Figure 2 organizes the workflow into parameter preparation, exact optimization and decision reporting. Observed tariffs and engineering transit-time estimates can populate the first layer directly. If a predictive model is available, it supplies estimates using the same units and indices. The optimization layer then filters paths, shares capacity and accounts for activation. The reporting layer returns quantities, activated operations, the objective, the best available bound and delivery slack.
The implemented procedure is stated below.

p.span: Algorithm 1 Capacity- and deadline-aware freight planning

td.p: 1. Construct a mode-compatible candidate-path catalogue and record shared resources, variable charges and fixed activation charges.
2. Obtain quantities, release times, delivery windows and nominal or protected path times.
3. Filter paths using Eq. (1) or Eq. (7). Stop with an eligibility diagnosis if any commodity has no eligible route.
4. Solve model (2)–(5), retaining the incumbent, dual bound, termination status and resource loads.
5. Verify demand conservation, capacity and activation consistency using the returned solution.
6. Report allocation, cost, resource utilization and minimum delivery slack. State whether the result is optimal for the specified catalogue or an incumbent with a remaining gap.
7. Re-solve relevant capacity, deadline and parameter-stress scenarios before committing to an operational change.

sec.p: A capacity proposal should be evaluated by the difference between two optimized objectives with otherwise identical inputs. A deadline concession should be evaluated by the allocation it enables, including newly incurred fixed charges. If either change modifies several resources at once, the analysis should report the combined scenario rather than interpreting a single linear-programming dual price as a universal value for a mixed-integer decision.

sec.title: 4.4. Performance measures and comparison design
sec.p: The optimization experiments record objective value, dual bound, final gap, resource loads and conservation residuals. A heuristic allocation is evaluated using the same quantities, costs, eligibility tests and capacities as the exact model. Its objective premium is

where, \(C_{\text{heuristic}}\) is the total cost of the feasible allocation obtained by a heuristic, and \(C_{\text{MILP}}\) is the total cost obtained by solving the mixed-integer linear programming model under the same inputs.

The paired sensitivity experiments alter one input family at a time. For each seed, capacity factors modify only non-fallback service capacities, while fixed-charge factors modify only activation charges. The reference objective at factor one provides the within-seed cost index. This design separates each factor from the changes in catalogue size used in the broader comparison.

Cost-error experiments keep times, deadlines and capacities unchanged and solve the model under perturbed unit costs. The selected plan is then evaluated using the original costs. This provides a direct test of decision regret on the same feasible set, as required by Eq. (11). The allocation methods used throughout these experiments are summarized in Table 3, including their decision procedures and stopping rules.

sec.title: 5.1. Corridor data and reproducible implementation
sec.p:
The reference corridor contains two commodities:
q 1
= 40 tonnes and
q 2
= 70 tonnes, both released at time zero. The three alternatives are direct road, road–rail–road and road–sea–road. Their unit costs, times and capacities are specified explicitly below. Rail-transfer operations cost 200 currency units at each terminal, and maritime-transfer operations cost 260 at each terminal. Thus the combined fixed charges are 400 and 520, respectively. Figure 3 and Table 4 state the complete numerical specification used by the path model.

caption.title: Complete corridor parameters for the path formulation

sec.p: For the arc-level representation, Path 2 comprises road legs with unit costs of 4 and 4 and transit times of 4 and 4 hours, together with a rail leg with unit cost 26 and transit time 22 hours. Path 3 comprises road legs with unit costs of 4 and 4 and transit times of 4 and 4 hours, together with a maritime leg with unit cost 19 and transit time 38 hours. Each of the four rail or maritime transfer operations has zero variable cost and zero additional duration in this synthetic corridor; its fixed activation charge is reported in Table 4. Access and egress arcs are specific to the corresponding modal operation and have capacities of 150 tonnes. The arc parameters sum to the path-level costs and transit times in Table 4.

The model and comparison methods were implemented in Python 3.12.14 using NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0 and the bundled HiGHS 1.8.0 solver on Linux x86-64. The execution host reported an Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C processor. Each generated mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) received a 15-second time limit and a relative mixed-integer programming (MIP)-gap target of 10
− 8
; other solver settings were left at their defaults. Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) and OpenMP thread environment variables were set to one. Computations were performed on a shared execution host. Recorded times cover the optimization call, excluding instance generation and plotting. Each instance was timed once, so small timing differences should not be interpreted as stable algorithm rankings.

sec.title: 5.2. Reference scenarios and feasibility checks
sec.p: Scenario A keeps 100 tonnes of rail capacity and 40-hour deadlines for both commodities. The sea path is ineligible. An optimal allocation sends 100 tonnes by rail and 10 by road, for

The individual commodity allocation is not unique because both commodities have identical costs and eligibility. One optimum places all 40 tonnes of commodity 1 and 60 tonnes of commodity 2 on rail, with the remaining 10 tonnes on road. The interpretation concerns aggregate mode loads; it does not require the solver to return this particular commodity split.

Scenario B raises rail capacity to 110 tonnes. All demand then uses rail, so
C B
= 34(110) + 400 = 4140. The capacity increase saves 240 currency units, or 5.48% of Scenario A’s cost. Scenario C restores rail capacity to 100 tonnes and reduces commodity 2’s deadline to 20 hours. Its 70 tonnes must use road, leaving commodity 1 on rail. The resulting cost is
C C
= 34(40) + 400 + 58(70) = 5820, 32.88% above Scenario A.

Three further scenarios test maritime eligibility and capacity shortfalls. Scenario D gives both commodities 50-hour deadlines. Sea becomes eligible and transports all 110 tonnes for 27(110) + 520 = 3490, 20.32% below Scenario A. Scenario E relaxes only commodity 2’s deadline to 50 hours. Commodity 1 remains on rail, while commodity 2 uses sea; the cost is 34(40) + 400 + 27(70) + 520 = 4170. Although sea has a lower unit cost, activating both intermodal operations limits the saving to 210 currency units. Scenario F combines a 20-hour deadline for commodity 2 with rail capacity of only 30 tonnes. Commodity 2 fills the 70-tonne road service and the remaining rail capacity cannot carry all of commodity 1, so the model is infeasible. Across these six scenarios, delivery deadlines and full shipment quantities are enforced as hard constraints; Table 5 brings together the corresponding settings, optimal allocations, minimum costs and feasibility outcomes.

All five feasible scenarios were solved to a reported zero relative gap. Their manually evaluated costs matched the solver objectives. Scenario F returned an infeasibility status. These checks confirm the intended response to activation costs, commodity-specific eligibility and shared capacity.

sec.title: 5.3. Capacity and deadline sweep
sec.p: The two-factor sweep varied rail capacity from 40 to 120 tonnes in one-tonne steps and commodity 2’s latest delivery time from 14 to 50 hours in one-hour steps. Commodity 1 retained its 40-hour deadline. The resulting 81 × 37 = 2997 settings were all solved; other parameters were held fixed. Figure 4 shows the objective surface and selected capacity slices.

caption.title: Exact capacity–deadline analysis over 2,997 settings: (a) objective surface; (b) capacity slices at selected deadlines

sec.p: For commodity 2 deadlines below 30 hours, rail and sea are both ineligible for that commodity. It therefore occupies the full road capacity. At every tested rail capacity of at least 40 tonnes, commodity 1 uses rail and total cost remains 5,820. Adding rail capacity has no value in this region because the commodity that could use it more extensively is excluded by its delivery commitment.

At deadlines from 30 through 45 hours, commodity 2 becomes rail-eligible but not sea-eligible. Cost decreases by 24 per added tonne of rail capacity until the 110-tonne demand is fully accommodated, in agreement with Eq. (8). The 100-to-110-tonne comparison is therefore one segment of a broader linear capacity-value region, not an isolated numerical coincidence.

At deadlines of at least 46 hours, commodity 2 can use sea while commodity 1 remains sea-ineligible. When rail capacity is only 40 tonnes, the rail-sea allocation costs 4,170 and avoids sending 70 tonnes by road. At 100 tonnes, it still costs 4,170 and remains preferable to the 4,380 rail-road plan. At 109 tonnes, however, the rail-road alternative costs 4,164 and becomes slightly cheaper because it avoids the extra maritime fixed charge. The equality occurs at 6,780 $-

sec.title: 5.6. Computational outcomes
sec.p:
Every generated MILP reached a reported zero relative gap within the 15-second limit, and all three heuristics returned feasible allocations. The maximum observed exact-model demand or capacity residual was below 7.2 × 10
− 13
tonnes. Median MILP-call times were 0.0022, 0.0054, and 0.4126 seconds for the three sizes; the maximum was 1.2790 seconds. These computation times are single-run measurements on the stated host. Allocation quality was assessed separately by comparing each heuristic with the exact objective; Table 6 reports the resulting mean cost premiums, together with the maximum ALS premium and the number of exact-objective matches achieved by ALS.

caption.title: Heuristic cost premiums against exact objectives for all 60 catalogues

sec.p: Across the three catalogue sizes, multiple ordering reduced the mean premiums from 2.69%, 10.60% and 17.95% under SG to 0.89%, 7.43% and 14.29%, respectively. ALS further reduced the corresponding mean premiums to 0.00%, 0.00% and 0.22%, respectively, and matched the exact objective in 49 of the 60 instances. Its largest premium was 1.26% (Figure 6). Thus most of the sequential rule’s avoidable cost was removed by joint flow reallocation and local activation changes. The remaining benefit of exact optimization was small for this generator; ALS therefore provides a more informative benchmark of that benefit than SG alone.

caption.title: Allocation-method comparisons on all 60 catalogues: (a) mean cost premiums for SG, MG and ALS; (b) individual ALS premiums with group medians shown in black

sec.p: Mean continuous-relaxation gaps for the 10 × 6, 30 × 12 and 60 × 24 catalogues were 0.003%, 0.229% and 0.790%, respectively, with an overall maximum of 1.713%. The combination of a strong relaxation and limited catalogue size helps explain the short exact-solver times. The experiment supports exact allocation as a practical baseline for catalogues of the tested sizes.

Catalogue size changes both the number of commodities and the number of services. It also changes aggregate non-fallback capacity because the generator assigns capacity as a fraction of demand to each service. Consequently, differences between size groups are descriptive rather than isolated commodity-count effects. The following paired tests address the separate effects of capacity and activation charges.

sec.title: 5.7. Paired capacity and fixed-charge experiments
sec.p: Five 30-commodity, 12-service catalogues were generated using the stated seeds, tight deadline mix and less-scarce capacity regime. Within each catalogue, non-fallback capacities were multiplied by 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, 1.25 and 1.50, with every other input unchanged. A second experiment applied the same five factors to fixed activation charges, leaving all capacities and other inputs unchanged. The fallback retained its full-demand capacity and zero charge throughout. The design therefore comprised two five-level experiments across five seeds, with a common factor-one reference for each seed. All 50 solves reached a reported zero relative gap, allowing the effects of the two factors to be compared against their respective within-seed reference solutions. Table 7 summarizes these effects through the cost indices, fallback shares in the capacity experiment and numbers of activated chargeable services in the fixed-charge experiment.

caption.title: Paired factor experiments over five seeds

sec.p: Reducing non-fallback capacity to half its reference value raised the mean within-seed cost index to 125.47, while increasing capacity by 50% reduced it to 94.13. Mean fallback shares changed from 41.94% at the half-capacity setting to 0.00% at the expanded setting. Because costs, quantities and deadlines were unchanged within each seed, these differences isolate the effect of available service capacity in the specified catalogue.

Fixed-charge changes produced a different response. At half the reference charge, the mean cost index was 93.16; at 1.5 times the charge, it was 106.13. The corresponding mean numbers of activated chargeable services were 5.4 and 4.6. These counts concern rail and maritime activations with positive charges, not the zero-charge road services. Figure 7 shows the cost and allocation responses.

caption.title: Paired capacity and fixed-charge experiments: (a) mean within-seed objective index; (b) mean fallback allocation

sec.p: For every seed, objective value was nonincreasing in capacity and nondecreasing in fixed-charge level. These monotonicity checks follow directly from the feasible-set and objective changes. Mode shares and activation counts need not follow an equally simple general rule: different services can substitute for one another as the optimal allocation changes.

sec.p: These results separate plan stability from cost stability. When several services have similar costs, estimation errors can move a sizeable fraction of tonnage while producing a much smaller realized objective loss. The bound remains a worst-case screening quantity rather than a prediction of that loss. Its interpretation is conditional on the unchanged feasible catalogue; transit-time errors require the separate deadline-protection analysis in Section 5.4.

sec.title: 6.1. Operational implications
sec.p: The corridor analysis distinguishes capacity shortages from eligibility restrictions. When both commodities can use rail, an extra tonne of rail capacity replaces a tonne of road transport and is worth 24 currency units until demand is accommodated. Tightening commodity 2’s deadline removes that substitution, so added rail capacity no longer helps it. An operator should therefore establish which shipments can use a proposed capacity increase before valuing the increase from modal unit-rate differences.

Fixed charges create a second decision boundary. In Scenario E, opening maritime operations saves only 210 currency units, although sea’s unit rate is seven currency units per tonne below rail’s. At 109 tonnes of rail capacity, the rail–road plan becomes cheaper because the small residual road allocation avoids a maritime charge. The paired experiments show the same distinction at catalogue scale: capacity factors alter access to inexpensive throughput, whereas fixed-charge factors alter the cost of opening services. They should be evaluated as different interventions.

The heuristic comparisons clarify the value of joint allocation. Multiple ordering reduced the sequential greedy premium, while LP reallocation and activation search removed most of the remaining difference. For the tested catalogues, exact optimization provided a certified optimum and resolved the residual allocation differences. Operational comparisons therefore need to account for both commodity ordering and the possibility of reallocating flows after service activation.

sec.title: 6.2. Parameter verification and planning stability
sec.p: Time and cost uncertainty call for different checks. A sea plan near the 50-hour deadline can become infeasible when its time estimate changes slightly; that is a service-eligibility issue. In the cost-error tests, the feasible set remains unchanged, so the selected plan can be reassigned without violating a deadline. The observed cost loss is then determined by how expensive the substitute services are under the original prices.

This distinction helps prioritize verification. Transit-time estimates near an eligibility threshold warrant checking before dispatch. Cost estimates warrant checking when they reverse the ranking of complete allocations after fixed charges are included. A large change in mode share alone does not prove a large economic loss: the cost-error results show substantial reassignment among near-substitute services. Conversely, a small final solver gap limits only the loss from unfinished optimization and says nothing about whether the supplied parameters are correct.

The results complement prediction-and-optimization research [7], [8], [24], [25], [26] by separating cost regret from deadline feasibility within an explicit freight allocation model. The exact and heuristic allocations provide computational reference points, while the bounded-error tests identify how changes in estimated costs propagate into service assignments and realized expenditure.

sec.title: 6.3. Limitations and extension priorities
sec.p: All instances are synthetic. The 2,997 settings are a systematic sweep of one small corridor, while the 60 catalogues vary service and commodity attributes within one common origin–destination structure. These experiments establish internal consistency and controlled comparisons, but they do not establish savings for a named carrier or scalability on a geographically complex network.

The formulation assumes divisible freight and independent delivery of each fraction. Containers, wagon formation, intermediate synchronization, scheduled departures, vehicle circulation and inventory costs can require additional variables and constraints. Restricted route catalogues can also omit valuable alternatives. Empirical deployment should therefore document how paths were generated and which operational commitments were included.

The proportional time bounds and uniform cost perturbations were chosen to expose sensitivities, not fitted to observed errors. ALS is a stronger reproducible comparator than SG, but it is still a limited local search. Its five-round cap does not establish one-toggle local optimality whenever the cap is reached. Larger network instances, additional optimization heuristics and carrier-data calibration would provide the next tests of external validity and computational performance.

sec.title: 7. Conclusions
sec.p: A path-based fixed-charge model was used to examine multimodal freight allocation under shared capacity and shipment-specific delivery windows. Its central decision relationship is conditional: capacity has value only for eligible demand, and a lower unit-cost mode need not be activated when its fixed charge exceeds the saving on the remaining tonnage.

The reference corridor quantified these conditions. Rail capacity was worth 24 per tonne over the relevant demand-limited region, a maritime plan cost 3,490 when both deadlines were 50 hours, and time inflation above 8.70% excluded that plan. The capacity–deadline sweep identified an additional reversal: with only commodity 2 sea-eligible, a rail–road allocation became cheaper above 108.75 tonnes of rail capacity because it avoided maritime activation.

The larger comparisons showed that the strength of the heuristic comparator affects the estimated benefit of exact optimization. ALS matched 49 of 60 exact objectives and reduced mean premiums to 0.00%–0.22%, while the paired experiments isolated capacity and charge effects. The 540 bounded-cost tests further showed that allocation movement can exceed realized cost regret by a substantial margin. Together, these results provide a reproducible operational baseline for capacity evaluation, deadline negotiation and input verification. Extending it to carrier data and explicit service schedules is the next application priority.

notes.title: Data Availability Statement
notes.p: The data supporting the findings of this study are included within the article, which specifies the corridor parameters, instance-generation rules and random seeds. All numerical data are synthetic and contain no individual shipment records. The experiment scripts, generated instances and solver outputs are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
